chunks: "Power sequencing is controlling the order and timing in which a board's supply rails come up, and go down.

Many chips need their rails in a defined relationship: core before I/O, say, or analog before digital, with I/O never more than a few hundred millivolts above the core, and a memory termination rail only after its supply.

So instead of letting all the regulators start whenever they like, you chain them: the power-good of one enables the next, or a sequencer or PMIC does it, and you hold reset until everything is stable.

Every I/O pin has ESD diodes to its supply, so if a pin is driven while that chip's rail is off, current flows backwards into the rail, partly powering the chip in an undefined state and sometimes triggering latch-up.
With the core up and I/O off, or the reverse, outputs may be in undefined states and fight each other on shared buses. Analog references need to be settled before converters run.

And from a power-integrity point of view, starting everything at once charges all the output and decoupling capacitors simultaneously: I equals C dV over dt on a milli-farad of capacitance is an amp, which can trip current limits or collapse the input rail.
Staggering the rails and controlling the ramps keeps the inrush manageable. The rules come from each chip's datasheet, and I'd verify the ramps on a scope across temperature."
